newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FEATURE - Portugal's elder statesman cannot avoid limelight.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Portugal's elder statesman cannot avoid limelight.

text.p: When he stepped down as president a year ago after a maximum two terms, Portugal's undisputed elder statesman Mario Soares certainly did not step out of the limelight.

The man whose presidency marked the period when Portugal finally put the turbulence of its 1974 revolution in the past, planned to dedicate himself to his foundation, set up to process the mountains of documents accumulated during his long political career, and to writing.
Once popularly known as 'King' Soares, for his regal manner, he had finished with domestic politics.
But the political world had not quite finished with him.

Soares already headed the Independent World Commission on the Oceans, set up in late 1995 to report to the United Nations on the state of the world's seas, and was more recently elected to the presidency of the European Movement, an non-governmental body aimed at furthering European integration.

"I am an active person, with much energy. I said that I would retire...and then things began to appear," he said, resignedly, in his office at the Mario Soares Foundation, set appropriately just across the road from parliament.

As a dedicated evangelist of European federalism, his election to the presidency of the European Movement, where he succeeded former French president Valery Giscard d'Estaing, will allow him to continue exercising one of his abiding passions.
"I want to see Europe advance towards supranational institutions, both political and federal. I am in favour of a United States of Europe," he said.
He had also been a logical choice for the commission on the seas, as Portugal will be the site of a world exhibition in 1998 -- Expo '98 -- which takes the oceans as its theme.
SOARES TO INVESTIGATE GOLD DEALINGS WITH NAZIS

But there was also another, undoubtedly more delicate challenge waiting in store -- one he certainly was not looking for -- and which is set to keep him at the forefront of public attention for months to come.

At the request of the government of Prime Minister Antonio Guterres, a fellow Socialist, and the Bank of Portugal, Soares will head a commission accompanying probes into controversial gold dealings with Nazi Germany during World War Two.
After Switzerland, Portugal was the largest recipient of Nazi bullion during the period.
"I am no accountant...but they told me they wanted somebody who commanded respect and was acceptable to all sides," he said.
"It is something grave, difficult. I cannot say that it is something I wanted to do but when the Jewish community contacted me, too. It was difficult to refuse."

The suspicion is that much of the gold received was plundered from countries overrun by Nazi troops. Worse, some of it may have come from the jewelry, watches and even teeth wrenched from the Jewish victims of the Nazi Holocaust
Portugal, which was neutral during the conflict, received some 100 tonnes of bullion either directly from Germany or from Switzerland between 1941 and 1943 in payment for exports.

It returned some four tonnes of gold under an accord with the Allied powers in the late 1950s at a time when the United States was anxious not to alienate Portugal's right-wing dictator Antonio Salazar, an ally in the Cold War.

But documents that have come to light in the United States and Britain in the past few months, with the expiry of a 50-year statute of limitations, have raised fresh questions about Portugal's wartime activities.

The role of the commission, on which Soares will be accompanied by two other personalities, one of whom will be a representative of the Jewish community, will be to lend moral authority to the conclusions of a probe being carried out by a Bank-appointed economic historian, Joaquim Costa Leite.
But the 73-year-old ex-president, who expects to hold his first meeting with Bank officials early this month, will say no more about the investigation.
"Nothing, until it is completed. That is a good rule," he says.
But there is no such reticence when it comes either to his foundation or to his vision of Europe.
SOARES HAS HOPES FOR EUROPE

On the latter, the veteran Socialist hopes that Tony Blair's election victory this month in Britain will redress what he sees as a political imbalance in Europe and help bring issues of social welfare and justice back into focus.

"It is not enough just to fulfill Maastricht criteria on inflation and budget deficits if there are 20 million people unemployed," he says, referring to European countries' obsession with satisfying economic tests for a coming single currency.
There is a pat on the back for Guterres, whose policies in the 18 months since he took power have so far combined economic rigour with a concern to create a fairer society, he says.

Soares' foundation contains over two million papers ranging from personal correspondence to political documents, all of which are being computerised to facilitate the work of future researchers seeking to mine a unique seam of information on contemporary Portuguese history.
In a corner of the mechanised vault housing the papers stands a battered old suitcase, a reminder of less certain and secure times.

It was in dozens of such cases hidden away in the houses of friends that Soares managed to preserve his papers and records during the years of right-wing dictatorship in Portugal that ended with the 1974 armed forces' revolt.
"That was how the secret police never got their hands on them," he said.
